query: For an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its creep resistance? Specify the governing factor and rationale, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, the operating boundaries under sustained stress, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The superior creep-resistance of nanocrystalline FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy (HEA) coatings arises because their very high configurational entropy and associated severe lattice distortion raise the activation energy for vacancy migration. This slows dislocation climb and grain/phase-boundary diffusion, thereby suppressing the dominant diffusion-controlled component of high-temperature plastic flow. Interfaces between the interpenetrating FCC and BCC domains further pin dislocations, but the rate-controlling step remains vacancy-mediated diffusion; hence the governing factor is the reduced effective lattice (and boundary) diffusivity imposed by chemical complexity.
generation.material_initial_state: ≈5 µm-thick as-deposited dual-phase (FCC + BCC) refractory HEA coating (e.g., Al0.3CrFeCoNi) on a steel substrate; equiaxed grains 80–120 nm; clean GBs; no second-phase oxides.
generation.intervention: Apply a constant uniaxial tensile stress of 0.3 · σ0.2 (≈30 % of the 0.2 % offset yield strength) for 100 h while holding the coating at 0.6 Tm (≈900 °C for the alloy).
generation.conditions: High-vacuum (≤10-5 mbar) or high-purity Ar atmosphere; sample temperature controlled to ±2 °C; initial dislocation density ≈1014 m-2; identical thermal history for all comparison samples.
generation.structural_mediator: High-density, nanoscale chemical-short-range-order (CSRO) clusters and coherent FCC/BCC interphase boundaries that pin dislocations and restrict vacancy migration paths.
generation.mechanism:
1. Severe lattice distortion and CSRO increase vacancy formation and migration energies (E_v + E_m).
2. Elevated diffusion activation energy (Q_creep ≈ 1.5 × that of pure constituent metals) slows vacancy flux.
3. Dislocation climb and GB/phase-boundary diffusion—rate-controlling for creep in nanocrystalline coatings—are therefore impeded.
4. Interphase boundaries add additional barriers, forcing dislocations to bow (Orowan) rather than climb, further reducing steady-state creep rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: At 0.6 Tm the steady-state creep rate (ė_ss) of the HEA coating will be at least one order of magnitude (≥10×) lower than that of an otherwise identical binary alloy coating (e.g., equiatomic NiCo) with the same grain size and texture. The stress exponent n will be ≥6 (vs. n≈3–4 for the binary), and the apparent creep activation energy (from 750–950 °C tests) will exceed that of lattice self-diffusion in Ni or Fe by ≥50 %.
generation.baseline: Creep behaviour of a compositionally simple, single-phase nanocrystalline FCC or BCC binary alloy coating fabricated and tested under identical conditions.
generation.boundary: Prediction holds for 0.4 Tm ≤ T ≤ 0.7 Tm and grain sizes 50–200 nm under stresses between 0.2 σ0.2 and 0.5 σ0.2. At T > 0.7 Tm or d < 30 nm, grain-boundary/phase-boundary sliding or Coble creep may dominate, invalidating the mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative values of vacancy migration energies in multicomponent HEAs remain scarce; precipitate-free assumption may not hold for all processing routes; oxide dispersions or carbide formation could provide additional strengthening, complicating attribution solely to sluggish diffusion.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of coatings: (A) the FCC/BCC HEA described above; (B) a binary alloy (NiCo) matching grain size, thickness, and prior deformation. Conduct constant-stress creep tests at 750, 825, 900, and 950 °C under σ = 0.3 σ0.2. Measure ė_ss after primary creep. Determine activation energy (Q_creep) from Arrhenius plots. Perform 63Ni or 55Fe tracer diffusion measurements at the same temperatures on both coatings to obtain lattice/GB diffusion coefficients.
measurements: Steady-state creep rate ė_ss vs. T and σ
Lattice and GB diffusion coefficients D(T)
Post-creep TEM for dislocation structures and interface morphology
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Hypothesis is falsified if (i) ė_ss(HEA)/ė_ss(binary) > 0.5 at any test temperature (i.e., HEA not at least twice as creep-resistant), OR (ii) Q_creep(HEA) ≤ Q_creep(binary) within experimental error (±10 kJ mol⁻¹), OR (iii) D_HEA(T) is not significantly lower (≤50 % reduction) than D_binary(T).
